title: Sit Spin
summary: A sit spin lowers the skating leg into a compact seated position while rotating around a relatively steady center.
timing_cues: The entry should settle before the main rotational moment begins.
The visual peak usually happens when the spin center is established and the body line looks stable.
stability_cues: Center drift reduces the clarity of the spin.
A steady upper body and consistent rotational axis are more important than raw speed.
duration_cues: If the spin exits too early, the movement can feel under-finished.
If the spin runs too long, it can break the planned musical transition.
coaching_cues: Prepare the entry edge early.
Keep the center controlled through the deepest part of the position.

title: Camel Spin
summary: A camel spin presents a longer body line with the free leg extended while rotating on a controlled axis.
timing_cues: The line should be visible early enough for the audience to read the shape.
The best musical moment often coincides with the fullest extension.
stability_cues: Hip level and center control are key to keeping the spin from traveling.
A broken upper-body line often makes the spin look unstable.
duration_cues: The line needs enough time to register visually.
Exiting too late can reduce musical precision.
coaching_cues: Reach the full line before chasing rotation speed.
Control the hip line to reduce travel.

title: Upright Spin
summary: An upright spin keeps the body more vertical and often relies on a clean center and leg line.
timing_cues: The acceleration into the spin should not rush past the musical accent.
The most readable moment is when the body is centered and visually tall.
stability_cues: Vertical balance and shoulder control influence whether the spin reads cleanly.
Traveling or wobbling weakens the effect.
duration_cues: A short upright spin may feel abrupt.
An overlong upright spin may feel repetitive if the music has already moved on.
coaching_cues: Build the center before increasing speed.
Keep the shoulders calm through the main rotation.

title: Two Foot Spin
summary: A two foot spin is a foundational training spin that uses both feet to help establish rotation, balance, and a readable center.
timing_cues: The spin should establish its center quickly instead of spending too long searching for balance.
The clearest visual moment comes when the rotation becomes calm and centered.
stability_cues: This element should still look centered even though it is more basic than a one-foot spin.
Excessive travel usually signals that the center was never fully found.
duration_cues: If it ends too quickly, the training value and visual read both drop.
If it lingers after the phrase moves on, the section can feel stalled.
coaching_cues: Find the center before trying to turn faster.
Keep the shoulders quiet while the rotation settles.

title: One Foot Spin
summary: A one foot spin asks for a clearer axis and more single-leg control than a two foot spin while still functioning as a basic spin family.
timing_cues: The entry should rise into the center without delaying the phrase.
The strongest moment is when the skater settles onto one foot and the rotation looks committed.
stability_cues: Single-leg balance and axis control matter more than speed here.
Traveling or repeated corrections make the spin look under-controlled.
duration_cues: The spin needs enough time to show that the center is truly established.
Leaving too early can make the element read like an incomplete setup.
coaching_cues: Commit cleanly onto the skating foot.
Protect the axis before accelerating the spin.

title: Scratch Spin
summary: A scratch spin is a fast upright variation that depends on a centered axis, a visually narrow line, and controlled acceleration.
timing_cues: The acceleration should crest with the intended musical lift instead of peaking too early.
The strongest visual moment often comes when the spin tightens and speed increases without losing center.
stability_cues: Fast rotation only reads well if the center stays compact and stable.
Shoulder swing or travel weakens the clean effect of the scratch position.
duration_cues: The fast section needs enough time to register as a highlight.
Resolving too soon can make the build feel unfinished.
coaching_cues: Build speed after the center is secure.
Keep the line narrow without letting the shoulders twist.

title: Layback Spin
summary: A layback spin relies on a clear back line, centered rotation, and enough duration for the stretched shape to read musically.
timing_cues: The full layback line should appear before or at the phrase peak, not after it.
The visual payoff is strongest when the back line opens clearly and stays readable through the accent.
stability_cues: The axis should remain centered even as the body opens backward.
A collapsing hip line or wandering center makes the spin lose authority.
duration_cues: The position needs enough hold time for the shape to register.
Exiting too early can make the dramatic line feel cut short.
coaching_cues: Open into the back line before the musical crest.
Keep the center steady while the upper body extends.

title: Biellmann Spin
summary: A Biellmann spin combines flexibility and rotation, asking for a high overhead line that still remains centered and musically placed.
timing_cues: The lift into the Biellmann line should land with a clear musical rise.
If the overhead shape arrives late, the main highlight can lose impact.
stability_cues: Pulling the leg higher should not cost the spin center.
If the axis travels while the position opens, the element looks less secure.
duration_cues: The overhead line needs enough time to be read as the climax of the spin.
A rushed exit can make the flexibility moment feel incomplete.
coaching_cues: Reach the overhead line before chasing extra speed.
Protect the axis while opening the flexibility position.

title: Combination Spin
summary: A combination spin changes positions within one rotational element and needs clear transitions between shapes.
timing_cues: Each position change should still respect the musical phrase.
The strongest moment often comes when the cleanest position is fully established.
stability_cues: Position changes can introduce center drift if transitions are rushed.
The center should stay readable even through variation changes.
duration_cues: Each position should be readable enough to matter.
Too much time in one phase can flatten the combination.
coaching_cues: Keep the transitions intentional between positions.
Do not sacrifice center control while changing shape.

title: Flying Spin
summary: A flying spin adds an airborne entry before the rotational phase and needs a clean moment of takeoff into center.
timing_cues: The airborne entry should not arrive after the intended accent.
The visual payoff is strongest when the landing into spin is immediate and centered.
stability_cues: The jump entry often introduces instability if the center is not found quickly.
Landing into a wandering rotation weakens the element.
duration_cues: The rotational phase still needs enough time to read after the entry.
If the spin resolves too quickly, the airborne setup dominates the element.
coaching_cues: Establish the center immediately after the airborne entry.
Avoid letting the jump entry delay the main rotational moment.

title: Toe Loop
summary: A toe loop uses toe-assisted takeoff timing and benefits from a clean rhythmic entry and controlled landing line.
timing_cues: The takeoff should line up with a clear beat or accent.
Late takeoff can make the jump feel disconnected from the phrase.
stability_cues: The landing edge and upper-body control influence whether the jump looks settled.
A rushed exit after landing usually reads unstable.
duration_cues: The landing flow should have enough continuation to connect into the next phrase.
coaching_cues: Set the pick rhythm early.
Protect the landing flow after touchdown.

title: Salchow
summary: A salchow uses a distinct edge-based setup and usually reads best when the takeoff is committed and the landing flows out cleanly.
timing_cues: The takeoff should grow out of the setup edge instead of arriving late to the phrase.
The landing moment often carries the strongest visual accent.
stability_cues: Landing control matters more visually than forcing speed.
Breaking the body line after landing weakens the jump.
duration_cues: The exit needs enough flow to reconnect with the choreography.
coaching_cues: Commit to the takeoff edge earlier.
Let the landing edge continue rather than stopping the flow.

title: Loop Jump
summary: A loop jump tends to reward compact timing and a stable landing line.
timing_cues: The takeoff should feel decisive and rhythmically clean.
A delayed jump entry can soften the intended accent.
stability_cues: Upper-body steadiness on landing affects the visual cleanliness of the jump.
A wandering landing line makes the jump look less secure.
duration_cues: The landing must connect into the next move without looking stalled.
coaching_cues: Keep the entry compact and decisive.
Protect the landing line before moving on.

title: Flip Jump
summary: A flip jump depends on a precise picked entry and a controlled landing phase.
timing_cues: The takeoff should not arrive after the main beat.
The jump usually reads strongest when the launch and landing both support the phrase.
stability_cues: The landing line should stay organized immediately after impact.
A shaky pickup into the jump can show up as instability later.
duration_cues: The landing continuation still needs enough room before the next element.
coaching_cues: Do not rush the pick before the accent.
Let the landing complete before forcing the next movement.

title: Lutz Jump
summary: A lutz jump often relies on strong approach control, committed takeoff timing, and a clear landing edge.
timing_cues: The setup needs enough time before the main launch.
If the takeoff comes late, the jump can miss the intended musical impact.
stability_cues: Approach composure and landing control both affect the cleanliness of the element.
A rushed landing exit weakens the effect.
duration_cues: The jump should leave enough continuation for the next phrase.
coaching_cues: Start the setup earlier if the takeoff keeps arriving late.
Hold the landing edge with more control.

title: Axel
summary: An axel often needs a committed forward entry, clear takeoff timing, and a confident landing flow.
timing_cues: The takeoff should match a clear rise or major accent.
Late launch tends to reduce the musical payoff.
stability_cues: Landing control and continuity are visually important for the axel.
A heavy landing or broken line weakens the phrasing.
duration_cues: The post-landing glide should have enough time to settle into the next movement.
coaching_cues: Prepare the entry earlier so the takeoff lands on the phrase.
Do not cut the landing exit short.

title: Jump Combination
summary: A jump combination links multiple jumps and needs both timing discipline and continued landing flow between parts.
timing_cues: The first jump should not consume the entire musical accent.
The connection between jumps needs to stay rhythmically alive.
stability_cues: Breaks in flow between jumps usually read as instability.
The landing of the first jump should support the takeoff of the second.
duration_cues: The connection needs enough time to read clearly without dragging.
coaching_cues: Protect the landing flow of the first jump.
Keep the connection rhythmically active between parts.

title: Step Sequence
summary: A step sequence is driven by rhythmic footwork, turns, and changes of direction that should stay alive with the music.
timing_cues: The section should stay rhythmically engaged instead of drifting away from the beat.
Important turns or accents should land near strong pulses.
stability_cues: The sequence does not need stillness, but it does need control through direction changes.
Chaotic upper-body movement can make the footwork look unclear.
duration_cues: If the sequence ends early, it can feel incomplete.
If it runs long, the next highlight can lose impact.
coaching_cues: Keep the rhythm visible through the feet and body line.
Use the strongest turns near clear musical pulses.

title: Choreographic Sequence
summary: A choreographic sequence often emphasizes expression, edge quality, and phrase design more than strict technical stillness.
timing_cues: The phrase should expand with the music instead of arriving after it.
The emotional peak should align with a visible gesture or highlight.
stability_cues: Expressive movement still benefits from controlled body lines.
Loose control can reduce the intended visual effect.
duration_cues: The phrase should breathe but still resolve within the musical section.
coaching_cues: Match the largest gesture to the main musical lift.
Do not let expressive timing become late timing.

title: Edge Transition
summary: An edge transition connects larger elements and should preserve flow, direction, and musical continuity.
timing_cues: Transitions should support the phrase instead of delaying the next element.
A late transition can push the main element off the music.
stability_cues: Even simple connecting edges should look controlled and intentional.
A broken line can make the program look unfinished.
duration_cues: The transition should be long enough to breathe but not so long that it drains momentum.
coaching_cues: Keep the line alive through the transition.
Use it to prepare the next element rather than to recover late.

title: Spiral
summary: A spiral relies on edge quality, extension, and enough duration for the line to be seen.
timing_cues: The line should reach full expression in time for the intended musical accent.
If the shape arrives late, the emotional peak is weakened.
stability_cues: Hip level and edge control determine whether the line reads cleanly.
Wobble or short holds make the spiral less convincing.
duration_cues: The line needs enough time to register visually.
coaching_cues: Reach the line earlier.
Hold the extension long enough for it to be seen.

title: Ina Bauer
summary: An Ina Bauer is often used as a musical and visual highlight built on edge control and openness of line.
timing_cues: The fullest shape should land with a strong rise in the phrase.
If entered too late, the dramatic effect drops quickly.
stability_cues: The edge and body line need to stay broad and controlled.
If the line collapses, the movement loses impact.
duration_cues: The position should breathe long enough to register before exiting.
coaching_cues: Open the line before the peak rather than after it.
Keep the edge broad and confident through the hold.

title: Spread Eagle
summary: A spread eagle is a wide edge-based transitional or highlight movement that depends on line and edge continuity.
timing_cues: The most open shape should align with the phrase highlight.
A late opening weakens the intended emphasis.
stability_cues: Edge security matters more than forcing a bigger shape.
Unclear edge control reduces visual confidence.
duration_cues: Too brief and it reads like a pass-through rather than a highlight.
coaching_cues: Let the shape open before the musical crest.
Prioritize clean edge continuation.

title: Lunge
summary: A lunge is a dramatic low transitional move that depends on line clarity, glide control, and a convincing held shape.
timing_cues: The drop into the lunge should arrive with the intended phrase emphasis.
If the lowest shape happens after the accent, the movement can lose impact.
stability_cues: The front knee, back leg line, and upper-body carriage should stay organized through the glide.
Wobble in the edge or a collapsing torso weakens the visual authority.
duration_cues: The line needs enough travel time to read as intentional.
Too brief and it can feel like a transition blur instead of a highlight.
coaching_cues: Drop into the lowest line before the phrase peak.
Keep the back leg extended and the torso calm through the glide.

title: Cantilever
summary: A cantilever is a highly dramatic field move that asks for deep knee bend, strong back control, and confident glide timing.
timing_cues: The deepest line should match the intended musical shock or release point.
A late drop can make the move feel disconnected from the phrase.
stability_cues: Because the body line is extreme, edge security and torso control are crucial.
Any visible loss of control quickly reduces the effect of the movement.
duration_cues: The move needs enough hold time to register, but not so much that the phrase loses momentum.
coaching_cues: Enter the deepest line with confidence rather than gradually collapsing into it.
Protect the glide and body tension while holding the shape.

title: Three Turns
summary: Three turns are foundational directional changes that should stay rhythmically clear and controlled.
timing_cues: The turns should speak with the beat if used inside a rhythmic phrase.
Late or blurred turns weaken the footwork texture.
stability_cues: The body should stay organized through the change of direction.
Extra upper-body noise can make the turn look messy.
duration_cues: The turn rhythm should remain consistent across the phrase.
coaching_cues: Let the turn happen on the beat, not after it.
Keep the torso quieter through the directional change.

title: Bracket
summary: A bracket is a more demanding one-foot turn that asks for edge clarity and calm upper-body organization through the directional change.
timing_cues: The turn should arrive crisply with the phrase instead of dragging after it.
If the bracket is late or blurred, the step passage loses sharpness.
stability_cues: The body should stay controlled while the edge and rotation oppose each other.
Visible recovery after the turn makes it read less confidently.
duration_cues: The rhythm around the turn should stay even so the step does not feel labored.
coaching_cues: Commit to the edge before the turn happens.
Keep the upper body organized so the turn reads clearly.

title: Rocker and Counter
summary: Rockers and counters are advanced one-foot turns that rely on edge command, clean directional timing, and visible control through the change.
timing_cues: The directional change should land close to the intended pulse or phrase inflection.
If the turn happens late, the footwork can feel reactive instead of authored.
stability_cues: These turns need a stable core and clean edge management more than visible speed.
A step that looks recovered rather than placed reduces confidence.
duration_cues: The turn sequence should keep the phrase alive without stretching the rhythm.
coaching_cues: Prepare the edge earlier so the change of direction arrives on time.
Stay stacked through the turn instead of correcting after it.

title: Mohawk
summary: A mohawk is a step-turn connection that often drives flow into larger elements or footwork phrases.
timing_cues: The entry and exit of the mohawk should preserve phrase direction.
A delayed mohawk can make the next element arrive late.
stability_cues: Clean transfer and edge control make the mohawk look intentional.
A sloppy transfer can break the movement line.
duration_cues: It should connect efficiently without becoming hesitant.
coaching_cues: Use the mohawk to carry flow, not pause it.
Keep the weight transfer clear and quick.

title: Choctaw
summary: A choctaw changes foot and edge in a more demanding way and should stay rhythmically clear inside step passages.
timing_cues: The directional shift should arrive clearly with the phrase.
A late choctaw can blur the rhythm of the sequence.
stability_cues: Body organization through the edge change is crucial.
If the step looks recovered instead of planned, the phrase loses confidence.
duration_cues: The change should be quick enough to preserve rhythm.
coaching_cues: Keep the change of edge decisive.
Do not let the directional shift lag behind the rhythm.

title: Twizzles
summary: Twizzles are traveling rotational steps that need rhythmic sharpness and upper-body control.
timing_cues: The first twizzle should arrive with a clear pulse.
Delayed initiation weakens the rhythmic effect.
stability_cues: Axis control and consistent body line keep twizzles readable.
Travel without control makes the sequence look rushed.
duration_cues: The turns should complete cleanly before the next phrase shift.
coaching_cues: Start the first rotation on the pulse.
Keep the body stacked while traveling.

title: Final Pose
summary: A final pose should resolve with the end of the phrase and hold long enough for the finish to register.
timing_cues: The pose should land at or just before the musical ending, not after it.
Reaching the pose late can weaken the final effect.
stability_cues: Stillness and line clarity matter more than movement intensity here.
A restless ending makes the finish feel incomplete.
duration_cues: The ending shape should be held long enough to read as intentional.
coaching_cues: Arrive into the pose before the sound fully resolves.
Hold the final stillness rather than releasing early.
